CIRCLE 239 · 2–8 NOVEMBER 2026

1 · Defynnog Yew

ANCIENT FRIEND of yOur Blooming Week

A living witness

A living witness, holding memory, resilience and the quiet power of deep time.

THE LIVING COMPANION

The Defynnog Yew grows in the churchyard at Defynnog in Powys, Wales. Its great age is difficult to establish precisely, particularly where trunks have hollowed or changed over time. Yews can live for many centuries.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Yew foliage, bark and seeds are poisonous. The red fleshy aril surrounds a toxic seed. Do not eat or forage any part of the tree.

2 · European Beech

TREE COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

The golden canopy

A graceful guardian of the woodland, weaving light, life and belonging.

THE LIVING COMPANION

European beech (Fagus sylvatica) is a deciduous woodland tree recognised by its smooth grey bark, spreading crown and autumn leaves. Beech mast provides food for some wildlife. Its fallen leaves become part of the woodland floor.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

A species lifespan does not establish the age of an individual tree. This illustration is not a food-identification guide.

3 · Ginger

PLANT COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

Hidden fire

REFLECTION: Hidden warmth, quiet growth, a new beginning.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Ginger (Zingiber officinale) is cultivated for its aromatic rhizome: an underground stem, not a root. It has long been used as a spice and in traditional practices. Some evidence supports particular ginger preparations for certain types of nausea.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Traditional medicinal use is not a promise of treatment. Claims about immune boosting, circulation, inflammation or travel sickness should not be presented as established benefits.

4 · Sycamore Helicopter

SEED COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

On the wind

A traveller of the air, carrying new life on the breeze.

THE LIVING COMPANION

The sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus) produces paired winged fruits known as samaras. Each samara carries a seed and spins or glides as it falls, helping it travel away from the parent tree.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

A samara is a winged fruit containing a seed. Do not infer a verified individual tree or wildlife sighting from this illustration.

5 · Ginkgo Leaf

LEAF COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

An ancient fan

A living fossil, bridging deep time to the present, with a leaf like a golden fan.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Ginkgo biloba is the sole living species of an ancient gymnosperm lineage. Its fan-shaped leaves become golden in autumn. The seed has a fleshy outer coat, but that coat is not a botanical fruit.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Ginkgo seeds contain toxins and can cause serious illness, including after cooking. Do not eat them. This image is not foraging guidance.

6 · Dahlia

FLOWER COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

Autumn’s colour

A flower of abundance, creativity and resilient beauty, bright even as the days grow shorter.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Dahlias are cultivated for their many flower shapes and colours. Their underground tubers help them survive between growing seasons. Open-centred forms can offer accessible pollen and nectar; tightly doubled flowers may offer less.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Historical edible or medicinal uses do not make ornamental dahlia plants generally safe to eat. No edible-tuber or treatment recommendation is made here.

7 · Rosehip

FRUIT COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

Winter’s gift

A wild gift of resilience, renewal and nourishment, carrying summer’s light into winter.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Rosehips form after rose flowers fade, and many persist into colder months. Some nourish wildlife. Different rose species and preparations have different characteristics. Many rosehips contain vitamin C, though amounts vary.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Do not treat rosehip as a medical treatment. The fine hairs around the seeds can cause irritation. This artwork is not a harvesting guide.

8 · Fly Agaric

FUNGUS COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

Woodland connections

A wild teacher of connection, transformation and the unseen life of the forest.

THE LIVING COMPANION

Fly agaric (Amanita muscaria) is a striking woodland fungus. Its underground mycelium forms ectomycorrhizal relationships with trees, exchanging resources across the root–fungus partnership. Its appearance has inspired art and stories in particular cultures.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

POISONOUS FUNGUS. Do not eat it or use it in food or home remedies. No preparation, recipe or dosage advice is provided.

9 · Slender-billed Northern Nutcracker

A visitor with seeds

A forest guardian of memory, planting tomorrow’s trees and feeding life through winter.

THE BIRD COMPANION

Northern nutcrackers (Nucifraga caryocatactes) cache seeds for later use. Forgotten seed stores can contribute to the growth of new trees. The name and ecological relationships should be kept distinct from an unverified sighting or subspecies identification.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

This painting is illustrative. Do not assign a precise subspecies, location or documented encounter without evidence.

10 · The Secret Garden

BOOK COMPANION of yOur Blooming Week

A garden reborn

EDITORIAL REFLECTION: Behind a closed door, life may still be waiting.

THE LIVING COMPANION

The Secret Garden is a 1911 novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett. In the story, Mary Lennox and friends tend a neglected garden. The book offers a literary exploration of attention, friendship, nature and renewal.

LIVING SCIENCE & CARE

Editorial reflection, not a quotation from the novel: “Behind a closed door, life may still be waiting.” This is a literary theme, not a claim that nature cures illness.
